body:
My initial reaction is that this is a spec bug. beforeunload has been sync [forever](https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=68215) (I'm sure @jstenback remembers this stuff perfectly), and then maybe accidentally got changed in https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/6315 . 
Now, if the target navigable has a cross-site document, then beforeunload needs to be async (these day, because of multiprocess), which does complicate things.  So one could also argue it should be always async, for consistency.
I wonder how webcompat risky this is.

> I wonder how webcompat risky this is.

Safari has had this event async for many years so probably not too risky.

From WebKit point of view, we'd much prefer for this event to remain async. Part of the reasoning is that it's already async for us. But importantly, if we make it synchronous to align with Blink/Gecko, it will force us to convert some async IPC into sync IPC, which is something we really try to avoid. The reason is that WebKit has a native client delegate call allowing them to prevent a navigation, I don't think we would want to figure to fire the `beforeunload` until **after** the native client app has decided to proceed with the navigation. Otherwise, it would be confusing to fire the `beforeunload` event, then have the client app block the navigation and no navigation actually happens.

I don't remember if we did it on purpose, but generally when we looked at the nav spec, we tried to make things consistently sync or async, and given that this cannot be consistently sync (eg due to child cross-site iframes when navigating a parent), and it was already async in Safari, we may have made it async on purpose.

But if it was by accident, it sounds like a good accident.

Neither Chrome nor Firefox fire `beforeunload` in the target document synchronously for [cross-agent](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#similar-origin-window-agent)-initiated navigations, so no solution we'd come to here will result in any implementation sending a sync IPC to fire `beforeunload` in a cross-agent target. Chrome and Firefox only fire it sync for same-agent-initiated navigations which I agree is weird. I'll investigate the Chromium impl a little more to see if there's any hope of changing this to match the spec, or if we should just have the spec reach across globals if they're in the same similar-origin window agent, to fire this event.
Whatever we do here would be something a bit new since either webkit hangs in some cases https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/12802 or it doesn't follow that part of the spec.

That problem ^^ is not peculiar to WebKit though, right? Sounds like any browser (and of course the spec) theoretically could be vulnerable to that, not just the ones that fire same-agent `beforeunload` event handlers async. I suspect that in practice, browsers have a mechanism to decrement the number of outstanding tasks they're waiting for if the document hosting those tasks is destroyed. Pretty sure that's how Chromium works, and probably the spec is just missing that part.

_I'm sorry this is long. No AI wrote any part of it, and it ends with a comprehensive proposal._

One thing I'm running up against in changing Chromium's behavior, is the behavior change incurred for navigations initiated _within_ a `beforeunload` handler. Consider this test: [`navigation-during-beforeunload.html`, subtest 3](https://github.com/web-platform-tests/wpt/blob/93a547af93e693c955d822a1aa2cc509280574de/html/browsers/browsing-the-web/unloading-documents/navigation-during-beforeunload.html#L70-L93):

1. Parent location-navigates child
2. Child's beforeunload handler navigates parent
3. Assert: parent's beforeunload is called, indicating that the parent's navigation isn't blocked by the child's beforeunload

In Chrome, (2) above results in the parent's `beforeunload` event being fired, which tricks the test into thinking that the parent navigation wasn't blocked. But after fired, Chrome synchronously attempts to fire the _child_'s `beforeunload` handler to see if it wants to cancel the parent navigation. We have a [re-entrancy guard around the handler](https://source.chromium.org/chromium/chromium/src/+/main:third_party/blink/renderer/core/dom/document.cc;l=4536-4543;drc=e40ec9d7e4e6462e2a6ee87f82da9fe9f776af35) so we don't fire it again (otherwise looping forever); this simulates "return false" and cancels the parent navigation. So Chrome passes the test because the parent's beforeunload is fired, making the test think it'll go through, but fails the intent since the parent navigation is actually blocked.

Safari's `NavigationDisabler` was recently page-global, meaning it used to block this navigation too (without even invoking the parent's beforeunload handler).

As far as I can tell, Chrome's "passing" result helped convince WebKit to match what it thought was Chromium's behavior; see https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/pull/62603:

> Fix by storing the disable count on the specific frame rather than the main frame. isNavigationAllowed() now checks only the target frame's own disable count. [Other] Sibling frames, ancestor frames, and descendant frames are all unaffected.

While this gives the impression that Safari matches Chrome, it actually made Safari diverge. Safari now passes the WPT correctly by not blocking the parent's navigation, while Chrome still blocks it (through less obvious means), yet wrongly passes the test. Here's the breakdown after way too many hours of messing around with this:

In Safari:
 - Parent navigates child
 - Asynchronously later, child's beforeunload handler runs, and navigates parent
 - Parent navigation goes through!

In Chrome:
 - Parent navigates child
 - Synchronously after, child's beforeunload handler runs, and navigates parent
 - Parent navigation is blocked, because we try and re-entrantly invoke child's beforeunload. When we can't, we block the navigation

I'm fixing the WPT so that Chrome will fail the test, and my change to Chrome making beforeunload event firing async in Chrome will pass it. But that means both Chrome and Safari will both have moved to this new behavior at the same time. How do people feel about that compat-wise? /cc @cdumez and @annevk who made the Safari change.

----

### Aligning on synchronous descendant beforeunload handlers

Chrome currently fires two kinds of `beforeunload` events synchronously:
 - Those on the same-origin target of a `location.href` assignment (motivating this issue)
 - Those on same-origin descendants of the target

I've been experimenting with Chrome firing the former asynchronously. So `sameOriginChild.location.href = foo;` would fire `sameOriginChild`'s beforeunload event asynchronously with respect to the assignment, but when it finally fires, it runs all of its same-origin children's beforeunload handlers in the same task, to see if they'd cancel.

The WPT I pointed out above actually relies on this. When the child beforeunload handler navigates its parent, the _parent's_ beforeunload handler runs asynchronously, and Chrome activates a frame navigation disabler on the parent. It's still active when it synchronously runs the child's beforeunload handler in the same task, so when the child tries to re-navigate the parent for a second time from _its_ beforeunload handler, the second parent navigation is dropped, which prevents the test from looping forever. The first parent navigation wins.

I noticed that Safari relies on the exact same mechanism: asynchronously-run beforeunload handlers _synchronously_ run their descendant tree's beforeunload handlers in the same task, and Safari's NavigationDisabler is active on the parent: https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/209e271d944ef2a3758bc25ca8ff8ab9bd149155/Source/WebCore/loader/FrameLoader.cpp#L4011-L4013 (if I'm reading this correctly).

Point is, whenever a beforeunload handler runs, all same-origin descendant beforeunload handlers run synchronously after, and are prevented from navigating the frame that kicked off the sync chain of same-origin beforeunload handlers. Since Chrome and Safari align on this part, we probably want to specify a few things:

 1. With respect to a navigation's initiator, the target's beforeunload handler always runs async
    - (This'll be new for Chrome, so lemme collect compat data)
 2. That while an async beforeunload handler is run, same-origin descendants have theirs run synchronously
    - This matches both Chrome and Safari. Changing this would be theoretically nice, but would require more complex re-entrancy mechanisms in the "browser process" of both implementations, for no benefit I can see.
 3. The top-most frame that the async beforeunload task was queued on, cannot be re-navigated navigated by its descendant handlers. That is, we specify Chrome's `FrameNavigationDisabler`, and Safari's `NavigationDisabler`.

**Thoughts on this proposal?**
